title: Up from 4% to 5%: up 1%?
hook: The rate went from 4% to 5%. That is a 1% rise. Or is it?

knows: that loans and savings have rates in percent
doesNotKnow: that 'up 1 point' and 'up 1 percent' are different statements
that a percent change depends on the starting value

misconception: A rate that goes from 4% to 5% rose by 1%.
objective: The learner can tell a change in percentage points (a distance on the scale) from a percent change (that distance divided by the start), and compute both.

claims.text: A rate rising from 4% to 5% rises by 1 percentage point, which is a 25% rise in the rate itself.
The same 1-point rise is +100% from 1%, +50% from 2% and +12.5% from 8%.
A percent change is the change divided by the starting value.
claims.source: Definition of relative (percent) change: (new − old) / old × 100.

claims.text: Careful writers call a change from 4% to 5% a rise of one percentage point.
claims.source: Style guides distinguish 'percentage point' from 'percent' for differences between rates (e.g. The Economist Style Guide, entry 'percentage points'; AP Stylebook, entry 'percentages').

recall.question: A survey says unemployment fell from 10% to 8%. A headline says "unemployment fell 2%". What is the more precise statement?
options: It fell 2 percentage points, which is a 20% fall
It fell 2%, the headline is exact
recall.why: 10 to 8 is a distance of 2 points on the scale. Relative to the start, 2 / 10 = 20%.
